notes: Conformance vectors for the `format_major` 3 protobuf-native atom
framing. Normative source: [RFCS.16]–[RFCS.19] in FACT_STREAM and [RDSC.4a]
in DSC_FORMAT, which is how the `clauses` arrays below cite them.
THIS FILE IS THE ONE HOME FOR THE BYTES: checks that compare two derived
views cannot see a hole the views share.
Consumers:
- specs/conformance/harness/runner.py, `pbf_framing` expect.kind — reads this
file directly and runs the groups Python implements.
- runtime/tests/libds/impl/pbf_vectors.h — GENERATED from this file by
scripts/gen_pbf_vectors.py and checked in, so the C tests need no JSON
parser. compiler/tests/test_gen_pbf_vectors.py fails if it drifts.
- third-party implementations: this file plus the clause text is the whole
contract. Nothing here depends on a DS header.
THE PREFIXES ARE HAND-COMPUTED, NOT EMITTED. A corpus generated by the
encoder under test would prove only that the encoder equals itself. Each
`prefix_hex` is worked out from [RFCS.19.1]'s grammar by hand; the ones
marked `protobuf_checked` are additionally checked against protobuf's own
serializer, which is the only independent implementation available here.
`prefix_hex` is everything BEFORE the body — outer tag, outer length, inner
tag, inner length. That is exactly `ds_pbf_prefix_size`'s contract, and the
reason it is a separate quantity: a major-3 prefix is variable-width, so a
caller must be able to ask its size before it packs the body ([RFCS.19.1]).

doc: framed = prefix_hex + body. `body_hex` gives the body literally;
`body_fill` gives {byte, len} for the length-varint boundary cases, where
a literal would be 16 KB of hex and the body's CONTENT is irrelevant —
only its length reaches the prefix.
`protobuf_checked` marks the rows whose body is a valid encoding of that
atom's message, so a driver can rebuild the container through protobuf and
compare. The fills are opaque bytes and cannot be; their job is the length
arithmetic, which the hand-computed prefix already pins.

vectors.name: fact_assert_empty
vectors.why: field 1, one-byte inner tag — the cheapest frame there is

vectors.name: fact_retract_empty
vectors.why: field 2: a frame that wrote the field number off by one reads as the atom beside it

vectors.name: clock_advance_empty
vectors.why: field 3, the third one-byte inner tag

vectors.name: realtime_contract_empty
vectors.why: field 128 — the inner tag grows to two bytes here

vectors.name: series_backend_interval_pulse_empty
vectors.why: field 129, beside 128; catches a tag varint that ignores the low bits

vectors.name: schema_def_empty
vectors.why: field 256: the tag's second byte carries a bit of its own, 0x10

vectors.name: stream_header_empty
vectors.why: opens a stream — [RFCS.19.4] reads the container type off this number

vectors.name: dsc_header_empty
vectors.why: opens a DSC — the other half of [RFCS.19.4]

vectors.name: alpha_node_empty
vectors.why: an ordinary structural atom

vectors.name: computation_error_empty
vectors.why: a live atom near the allocation frontier, in the two-byte-tag range. What the row is FOR is a live atom at the frontier, so it moves when the frontier does

vectors.name: dsc_header_format_major_3
vectors.why: a NON-EMPTY body: an empty one cannot catch a length mis-encoding, because the length is zero either way. 08 03 is DscHeader.format_major = 3

vectors.name: ds_source_body_1
vectors.why: the smallest non-empty body

vectors.name: ds_source_body_126
vectors.why: the OUTER length crosses 127 first, at a body of 126 — an implementation that sizes the outer varint from the body length instead of the inner length gets this one wrong and the next one right

vectors.name: ds_source_body_127
vectors.why: last one-byte inner length

vectors.name: ds_source_body_128
vectors.why: first two-byte inner length — both varints grow

vectors.name: ds_source_body_16383
vectors.why: last two-byte inner length; the outer is already three

vectors.name: ds_source_body_16384
vectors.why: first three-byte inner length

doc: One container per vector, with every verdict a reader owes about it:
the container type, the atoms in order, and the step result AFTER the
last atom.
`terminal` is the distinction [RFCS.19.2] exists to make. `eof` covers a
clean end AND a half-written tail: a recording is appended to while it is
read, so a reader that called a partial trailing atom corruption would
fail on every live stream. `malformed` is for bytes no further append can
rescue.
`protobuf` records what protobuf's own parser does with the same bytes.
It is NOT always `accepts`, and the disagreements are the point. There
are two classes, and an implementer who reads only the `accepts` rows
will build the wrong reader:
1. TRUNCATION — protobuf refuses, DS returns the atoms it got. DS is
deliberately WEAKER: a recording is appended to while it is read, so
a reader that called a half-written tail corruption would fail on
every live stream ([RFCS.19.2], and [RFCS.19.8] rests on it).
2. `empty_atom_is_malformed` — protobuf ACCEPTS: an Atom with no oneof
member set is a valid message. DS refuses it. DS is STRICTER here,
because an atom with no identity is nothing to dispatch on ([RFCS.19.3]).

vectors.name: empty
vectors.why: zero bytes is not a malformed container, it is no container

vectors.name: dsc_header_only
vectors.why: the minimum DSC: [RFCS.19.4] takes the container type from the first atom's NUMBER, with no magic anywhere on the wire

vectors.name: stream_header_then_inject
vectors.why: the other container type, and the two-level frame twice in a row

vectors.name: two_atoms_dsc
vectors.why: concatenation IS the container

vectors.name: dsc_header_with_body
vectors.why: a body the reader must hand back unchanged and un-copied

vectors.name: truncated_outer_length
vectors.why: [RFCS.19.2] — a lone outer tag with no length. One byte of a live recording; the reader ends at the last COMPLETE atom

vectors.name: truncated_inner_body
vectors.why: the outer length promises five bytes and four arrived. Note the container is UNKNOWN: the type comes from the first atom, and there is no first atom yet

vectors.name: truncated_mid_length_varint
vectors.why: the buffer ends INSIDE a varint, with its continuation bit set. Distinct from the two above: a length-prefix reader that only bounds-checks after decoding reads past the end here

vectors.name: empty_atom_is_malformed
vectors.why: a complete frame around an Atom with no oneof member. Valid protobuf, no identity to dispatch on — the one vector where DS is STRICTER than protobuf

vectors.name: group_wire_type_is_malformed
vectors.why: field 263 with wire type 3. proto3 has no groups, so no further bytes make this an atom — malformed, NOT the truncation of [RFCS.19.2]

vectors.name: field_zero_is_malformed
vectors.why: field 0 is not assignable in any protobuf schema. It also catches zero-fill: a run of 0x00 decodes as field 0 / wire 0 and would otherwise scan forever as empty varint fields

vectors.name: legacy_magic_container
vectors.why: a format_major 2 DSC — ASCII 'DSCO' + a u32-BE length. 0x44 is field 8 / wire type 4, and proto3 has no groups, so it is malformed. A major-3 reader does not classify these bytes as another format: with no converter there is exactly one refusal, and classifying provenance from leading bytes is a guess whichever way the ranges fall

vectors.name: foreign_bytes
vectors.why: 0xFF is field 31 / wire type 7, which does not exist. Same verdict as the format_major 2 row above and by the same route — the reader has one question, not three
